result:
Solution 3's construction checks out, so its answer of 12 is plausible. Its impossibility argument for 13 is not rigorous, and my own check does not establish the upper bound either.

**Solution 3's construction for 12.** Put one bouncing assistant on each of the 12 edges. Every assistant first travels outward from the start vertex, so on any shared transit edge all traffic moves in the same direction and the faster assistant stays ahead. I checked the timing of each stage:
- Level-2 transiters (speeds 1024 and up) clear the level-1 edges at or before the moment a level-1 bouncer first reaches the far vertex of its own edge. They exit at a vertex, so there is no interior collision.
- Level-1 transiters (speeds 16 to 512) clear the level-0 edges long before the level-0 bouncers turn back.
- Once the transit phase is over, every assistant bounces on its own edge, so no two share an edge.

So n = 12 works.

**Why 13 looks unattainable.** Two assistants bouncing on the same edge always meet at an interior point. For speeds 2 and 4, they meet at position 2/3. Sharing a simple cycle also costs edges. A 6-cycle holds only 3 consecutive speeds (the condition is that 2^d − 1 divides the cycle length), and it uses 6 edges to do so. That is worse than one bouncer per edge. I did not find a clever sharing scheme that beats 12, but I did not prove one is impossible either.

**Solution 1 (answer 8).** Its construction packs assistants into edge groups that are less efficient than one bouncer per edge. Since 12 is achievable, 8 is not the maximum.

**Solution 2 (answer 3).** It only considers shared directed cycles and dismisses bouncing strategies without justification. The one-per-edge bouncing construction achieves far more than 3, so this is wrong.

VERDICT 1: REJECT
VERDICT 2: REJECT
VERDICT 3: ACCEPT
